title: Pharmaceutical and Medicinal Chemistry
description: Physicochemical properties and drug action, structure–activity relationships, drug stability and prodrugs, and the medicinal chemistry of major drug classes.

topics.title: Physicochemical Properties and Drug Action
topics.summary: Lipophilicity, partition coefficient, pKa, solubility and Lipinski's rule of five.

notes.b: Drug action depends on reaching the target and binding to it. Lipophilicity is measured by the partition coefficient (log P, octanol/water); moderate lipophilicity favours oral absorption and membrane crossing, while very high log P reduces solubility and increases tissue accumulation. pKa determines the proportion ionised at a given pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch): for an acid, pH − pKa = log([ionised]/[un-ionised]). Salt formation improves water solubility (e.g. hydrochlorides of bases; sodium salts of acids). Lipinski's rule of five predicts poor oral absorption when a molecule has more than 5 H-bond donors, more than 10 H-bond acceptors, molecular weight above 500 Da, or log P above 5.
k: Lipinski: ≤5 donors, ≤10 acceptors, MW ≤500, log P ≤5

notes.b: Drugs bind targets through ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, hydrophobic interactions and (rarely) covalent bonds (e.g. aspirin acetylating COX, penicillin acylating transpeptidases, organophosphates phosphorylating acetylcholinesterase). The pharmacophore is the arrangement of features necessary for activity. Bioisosteres are groups with similar physicochemical properties used to modify drugs (e.g. replacing –COOH with tetrazole in losartan). Stereochemistry matters because receptors are chiral.
k: Most binding is reversible (ionic, H-bond, hydrophobic)

topics.title: Structure–Activity Relationships and Prodrugs
topics.summary: SAR principles, QSAR, prodrug strategies and drug stability.

notes.b: Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies change parts of a lead molecule to see how activity changes, identifying groups essential for activity and allowing optimisation of potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Quantitative SAR (QSAR) relates activity mathematically to physicochemical parameters (e.g. Hansch analysis using log P, electronic σ and steric parameters). Examples: adding a bulky N-substituent to adrenaline increases β-selectivity (isoprenaline, salbutamol); methylation of the catechol ring (as in salbutamol's saligenin) prevents COMT metabolism, allowing oral use.

A prodrug is inactive until metabolised to the active drug. Reasons: improve absorption (enalapril → enalaprilat; valaciclovir → aciclovir), target sites (levodopa crosses the blood–brain barrier then becomes dopamine), prolong action, or reduce toxicity or bad taste. Other prodrugs: codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), clopidogrel, proguanil → cycloguanil, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine → 6-mercaptopurine, and artemisinin derivatives (artesunate and artemether → dihydroartemisinin). Drugs degrade by hydrolysis (esters and amides — aspirin, penicillins), oxidation (adrenaline, vitamin C), photolysis (nifedipine, sodium nitroprusside) and racemisation; stability is improved by suitable pH, antioxidants, light-resistant packaging, low moisture and cool storage.
k: Prodrugs: enalapril, valaciclovir, levodopa, codeine, clopidogrel

topics.title: Medicinal Chemistry of Antimalarials
topics.summary: Quinolines, artemisinins, antifolates and ACT combinations used in Nigeria.

notes.b: 4-Aminoquinolines (chloroquine, amodiaquine) accumulate in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and inhibit haem polymerisation to haemozoin, so toxic free haem kills the parasite; widespread chloroquine resistance (PfCRT mutations) ended its first-line use for falciparum malaria in Nigeria. Quinine (a quinoline methanol from Cinchona) and mefloquine act similarly. 8-Aminoquinolines (primaquine, tafenoquine) kill liver hypnozoites of P. vivax/ovale and gametocytes but cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Artemisinins contain an endoperoxide bridge activated by iron/haem to generate free radicals, killing parasites rapidly. Antifolates: pyrimethamine (DHFR inhibitor) with sulfadoxine (dihydropteroate synthase inhibitor) — SP used for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy.
k: Primaquine: hypnozoites; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency

notes.b: WHO and Nigeria's national malaria treatment guidelines recommend artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) for uncomplicated falciparum malaria — artemether–lumefantrine (first line, taken with fatty food to improve lumefantrine absorption), artesunate–amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine and others — combining a fast-acting artemisinin with a longer-acting partner to prevent resistance. Severe malaria is treated with injectable artesunate. Artemisinin monotherapy is discouraged. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention uses sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine in the Sahel region for young children.
k: SMC: SP + amodiaquine in the Sahel

topics.title: Medicinal Chemistry of Antibacterials
topics.summary: β-lactams, sulphonamides, quinolones and others: structures, mechanisms and resistance.

notes.b: Penicillins contain a β-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring (6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus); cephalosporins have a β-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring (7-aminocephalosporanic acid). They acylate penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking. Benzylpenicillin is acid-labile (given by injection); phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) is acid-stable. Bulky side chains (flucloxacillin) resist staphylococcal β-lactamase; an amino group (ampicillin, amoxicillin) broadens the spectrum. β-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav, sulbactam, tazobactam) protect partner β-lactams. Carbapenems (meropenem) are very broad.

Sulphonamides are structural analogues of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) that competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase; with trimethoprim (DHFR inhibitor) they give sequential blockade (co-trimoxazole). Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; they chelate metal ions (avoid antacids) and can damage developing cartilage. Aminoglycosides are polycationic, poorly absorbed orally, nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Tetracyclines chelate calcium (tooth staining in children). Macrolides have large lactone rings. Nitroimidazoles (metronidazole) are activated by reduction in anaerobes to DNA-damaging radicals.

topics.title: Medicinal Chemistry of CNS and Cardiovascular Drugs
topics.summary: Benzodiazepines, opioids, local anaesthetics, β-blockers and ACE inhibitors: structure and action.

notes.b: Benzodiazepines (1,4-benzodiazepine nucleus; e.g. diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam) enhance GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency; flumazenil is the antagonist. Opioids share a morphine-like pharmacophore (tertiary nitrogen, aromatic ring, quaternary carbon); converting the N-methyl group of morphine to N-allyl gives the antagonist nalorphine/naloxone. Local anaesthetics have a lipophilic aromatic group, an intermediate ester or amide chain, and a hydrophilic amine; esters (procaine, benzocaine) are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and more allergenic (PABA metabolite), while amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine — two 'i's) are metabolised in the liver. Local anaesthetics work poorly in infected (acidic) tissue because more drug is ionised.
k: Benzodiazepines ↑ GABA-A Cl− channel opening frequency
LAs work poorly in acidic infected tissue

notes.b: β-blockers are aryloxypropanolamines (propranolol, atenolol, metoprolol) with an isopropyl or tert-butyl group on the amine for β-receptor affinity; hydrophilic atenolol is renally excreted and crosses the blood–brain barrier less. ACE inhibitors were designed from snake venom peptides: captopril (thiol group — taste disturbance, rash), enalapril and lisinopril (carboxylate). Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan) contain a biphenyl tetrazole. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine) are light-sensitive. Statins mimic the HMG-CoA intermediate.
k: Captopril: thiol group; derived from snake venom
